title: Bidirectional BFS in Singapore: Meeting in the Middle ⚡
description: Watch Bidirectional BFS route across Marina Bay by launching two BFS searches—one from start and one from goal—until they meet. This meeting-in-the-middle approach slashes the explored graph area and speeds up shortest-path finding.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half — How launching two simultaneous searches doubles graph traversal speed ⚡

Imagine routing from Marina Bay Sands to Gardens by the Bay. Instead of pushing one BFS frontier through the city maze, Bidirectional BFS runs two BFS waves at once: 
1) Forward BFS from the start node.
2) Backward BFS from the goal node. 
3) The moment the frontiers intersect, you reconstruct the shortest path.

Deep technical breakdown (the “why it’s faster” part):
- Classic BFS explores outward layer by layer from the start.
- With branching factor b and shortest path length d, BFS explores ~O(b^d) states.
- Bidirectional BFS explores from both ends, effectively reducing depth to ~d/2 from each side.
- That yields ~O(b^(d/2) + b^(d/2)) ≈ O(b^(d/2))—a dramatic search-space cut.
- You also need careful implementation: track visited sets separately (or store parents per direction) and detect intersection efficiently.

Takeaway: If your problem asks for the shortest path in an unweighted graph and bidirectional expansion is valid, meeting in the middle is a real graph optimization.

Debate question: In your coding interviews, would you prefer clarity (single BFS) or speed (Bidirectional BFS) when both are correct?
